units.title: Module 1: Development of practical skills in physics

topics.title: 1.1 Practical skills assessed in a written examination

outcomes.text: Design an experiment for a practical problem, choosing suitable apparatus, equipment and techniques.
Identify the variables that have to be controlled in an investigation.
Judge whether an experimental method is suitable for reaching the expected outcome.
Use a wide range of practical apparatus and techniques correctly.
Choose appropriate units for measurements.
Present observations and data in a suitable format.
Process, analyse and interpret qualitative and quantitative results, reaching valid conclusions.
Apply suitable mathematical skills to analyse quantitative data.
Give answers to an appropriate number of significant figures.
Plot graphs with labelled axes and scales, and measure gradients and intercepts.
Evaluate results and draw conclusions from them.
Spot anomalous measurements in experimental data.
Describe limitations of an experimental procedure.
Discuss precision and accuracy, margins of error, percentage errors and apparatus uncertainties.
Suggest improvements to procedures and apparatus to refine the design.

topics.title: 1.2 Practical skills assessed in the Practical Endorsement

outcomes.text: Apply investigative approaches and methods to practical work, including solving problems in a practical context.
Use practical equipment and materials safely, identifying hazards and minimising risks.
Follow written instructions in practical work.
Make and record observations and measurements.
Keep suitable records of experimental activities.
Present information and data in a scientific way.
Use software and tools to process data, research and report findings.
Use online and offline research sources such as websites, textbooks and printed material.
Cite sources of information correctly.
Use a wide range of instruments, equipment and techniques suited to the content.
Use analogue apparatus for length, temperature, pressure, force, angle and volume, interpolating between scale marks.
Use digital instruments such as multimeters to measure time, current, voltage, resistance and mass.
Improve accuracy by timing many oscillations or using a fiducial marker, set square or plumb line.
Use a stopwatch or light gates for timing.
Use callipers and micrometers, digital or vernier, for small distances.
Build circuits from diagrams using DC supplies, cells and components, including polarity-sensitive ones.
Design, construct and check circuits with DC supplies, cells and components.
Use a signal generator and oscilloscope, including volts per division and time-base settings.
Generate and measure waves with microphone and loudspeaker, ripple tank, vibration transducer or microwave source.

subtopics.title: Using apparatus: light, ICT and radiation

outcomes.text: Use a laser or light source to investigate interference and diffraction.
Use computer modelling, data loggers with sensors, or software to collect and process data.
Use ionising radiation and detectors.
Explain what affects the accuracy and uncertainty of measurements.
Recognise the largest source of uncertainty in a measurement and why it matters.
Use SI units and prefixes, standard form, and angles in degrees and radians.
Use the terms accuracy, precision, resolution, sensitivity, response time, uncertainty and systematic and zero error correctly.
Sketch and interpret distributions of repeated measurements to estimate the mean or median, spread and outliers.
Use scatter graphs, pie charts, log graphs and uncertainty bars to judge whether data are valid.
Calculate uncertainty of data, mean, range, spread and percentage uncertainty, and best-fit gradients and intercepts with uncertainty.
Estimate the uncertainty when data are added, subtracted, multiplied, divided or raised to powers, using extreme values.
Estimate the sizes of everyday quantities.
Explain how a thin converging lens forms a real image by changing the curvature of incoming wavefronts.
Use the terms pixel, bit, byte, focal length, power, magnification, resolution, sampling, signal, noise and polarisation correctly.
Sketch and interpret light passing through a converging lens using wavefronts and rays.
Practical: determine the power or focal length of converging lenses.
Explain how a computer stores an image as an array of numbers and how editing enhances it (brightness, contrast, noise, edges, false colour).
Explain digitising a noisy signal and the pros and cons of digital signals.
Sketch and interpret waveform diagrams.
Calculate the information in an image as pixels times bits per pixel.
Describe the evidence that electromagnetic waves can be polarised.
Practical: observe polarisation effects with microwaves and light.
Calculate lens power P = 1/f as the change of wavefront curvature.
Use 1/v = 1/u + 1/f for thin converging lenses with real images.
Calculate linear magnification as image height over object height, equal to v/u.
Use v = fm, including f = 1/T for waves.
Use N = 2^b to link bits to number of levels, and b = log2 N.
Apply the rule that the sampling rate must exceed twice the highest signal frequency.
Calculate the transmission rate as samples per second times bits per sample.
Represent digitisation of an analogue signal graphically for a given number of levels.
Use b = log2(V total / V noise) to find the bits that are useful above noise.
Explain current as the flow of charged particles.
Explain potential difference as energy per unit charge.
Explain resistance and conductance, including series and parallel combinations.
Use R = V/I, G = I/V, V = W/Q = P/I, P = IV = I squared R, W = VIt and V = E - Ir.
Use I = delta Q over delta t and combine resistances or conductances in series and parallel.
Explain internal resistance and the meaning of e.m.f.
Explain how power is dissipated in electric circuits.
State the relationship between potential difference and current in ohmic resistors (Ohm's law).
Describe electrical behaviour of metals, semiconductors and insulators using the number density of mobile charge carriers.
Explain how a potential divider works.
Calculate the output of a simple potential divider using Vout = R2/(R1+R2) times Vin and V1/V2 = R1/R2.
Explain conservation of charge and energy as Kirchhoff's first and second laws.
Use circuit terms such as e.m.f., resistivity, conductivity and charge carrier number density, and standard circuit symbols.
Sketch and interpret I-V graphs and graphs of resistance or conductance against temperature for ohmic and non-ohmic parts.
Use R = rho L / A and G = sigma A / L for resistivity and conductivity.
Practical: investigate I-V characteristics of ohmic and non-ohmic components.
Practical: determine the resistivity or conductivity of a metal.
Practical: use potential divider circuits with sensors such as a thermistor or LDR.
Practical: calibrate a sensor or instrument.
Practical: find the internal resistance of a cell.
Describe elastic and plastic deformation and fracture.
Use terms stress, strain, Young modulus, tension, compression, fracture and yield stress, stiff, elastic, plastic, ductile, hard, brittle, tough, strong.
Sketch and interpret force-extension and stress-strain graphs up to fracture.
Describe direct evidence of particle size and spacing, such as STM images or the oil drop experiment.
Explain behaviour of metals, ceramics and polymers, including dislocations and slip, brittle fracture and polymer chain entanglement.
Interpret tables and diagrams comparing materials, and images of material structures.
Describe one method of measuring Young modulus and fracture stress.
Calculate stress, strain and Young modulus E = stress/strain.
Practical: plot force-extension graphs for springs, rubber bands and polythene strips.
Practical: determine Young modulus of a metal wire.
Use F = kx and energy stored 1/2 kx squared as the area under a force-extension graph.
Explain how standing waves form from waves travelling in opposite directions, including graphical treatment.
Calculate wavelengths of standing waves, ignoring end corrections.
Practical: use an oscilloscope to find frequencies.
Practical: superposition experiments with strings, sound, light and microwaves.
Practical: find the speed of sound in air using stationary waves in a resonance tube.
Explain interference of waves from two slits.
Explain refraction of light at a plane boundary through the change of light speed, using the wave model.
Use Snell's law, n = sin i / sin r, equal to the ratio of wave speeds.
Practical: determine the refractive index of a transparent block.
Explain diffraction of waves through a narrow aperture.
Explain diffraction by a grating.
Calculate path differences for double slits and gratings using n lambda = d sin theta with a distant screen.
Practical: measure the wavelength of light with a double slit and a grating.
Describe evidence that photons exchange energy in quanta E = hf, such as LEDs, photoelectric effect and line spectra.
Calculate photon energy E = hf across the spectrum.
Practical: determine the Planck constant using different coloured LEDs.
Explain that quanta arrive with a probability found by combining amplitude and phase over all possible paths.
Describe how electron diffraction shows electrons behave quantum mechanically.
Calculate a particle's de Broglie wavelength lambda = h/p.

Use terms phase, phasor, amplitude, probability, interference, diffraction, superposition, coherence, path difference, intensity, electronvolt, refractive index, work function and threshold frequency.
Use vectors to represent displacement, velocity and acceleration.
Draw vector addition and changes in vector size and direction graphically.
Add two vectors graphically and algebraically, for perpendicular vectors.
Describe the trajectory of a body moving with constant acceleration in one or two dimensions.
Describe how to measure displacement, velocity and acceleration.
Use the constant acceleration equations v = u + at, s = ut + 1/2 at squared and v squared = u squared + 2as.
Explain the independent effects of perpendicular components of a force.
Resolve a vector into two perpendicular components.
Explain how to calculate work done, including when force is not parallel to displacement.
Explain the principle of conservation of energy.
Explain power as the rate of energy transfer.
Calculate work done W = F s, or F s cos theta at an angle.
Calculate kinetic energy 1/2 mv squared.
Calculate gravitational potential energy mgh.
Calculate power as energy over time and as Fv.
Explain Newton's laws of motion.
Explain conservation of momentum, with Newton's third law as a consequence.
Calculate momentum p = mv.
Use F = ma as rate of change of momentum for constant mass.
Apply conservation of momentum to one-dimensional problems.
Use terms displacement, speed, velocity, acceleration, force, mass, vector, scalar, work, energy, power, momentum and impulse.
Sketch and interpret graphs of accelerated motion: slopes of displacement-time and velocity-time graphs and area under velocity-time.
Model changes of displacement and velocity in small time steps for zero or constant resultant force.
Practical: investigate motion and collisions of trolleys or gliders using timers, light gates, loggers or video.
Practical: determine the acceleration of free fall.
Practical: investigate terminal velocity of a ball bearing in liquid or paper cones in air.

units.title: Module 5: Rise and fall of the clockwork universe

outcomes.text: Explain capacitance as the ratio C = Q/V.
Explain the energy stored on a capacitor, E = 1/2 QV.
Interpret the area under a Q-V graph as capacitor energy.
Calculate with C = Q/V, I = dQ/dt and E = 1/2 QV = 1/2 CV squared.
Explain why charge on a discharging capacitor decays exponentially: the removal rate is proportional to the charge left.
Use the terms time constant for a capacitor circuit.
Sketch and plot exponential curves on linear or logarithmic scales, including capacitor charging and discharging.
Calculate the time constant tau = RC from data, with Q = Q0 e^(-t/RC).
Solve dQ/dt = -Q/RC by numerical or graphical methods; use charging and discharging equations for Q, V and I.
Practical: investigate charging and discharging of a capacitor with meters and loggers.
Explain radioactive decay as a random process with a fixed probability: dN/dt = -lambda N.
Use terms activity, decay constant, half-life, probability and randomness.
Express rate-of-change-proportional-to-amount relationships in words, formulae and diagrams.
Calculate activity and half-life from data, using T1/2 = ln 2 / lambda.
Solve dN/dt = -lambda N numerically or graphically, with N = N0 e^(-lambda t).
Practical: determine the half-life of an isotope such as protactinium.
Explain simple harmonic motion of a mass with restoring force proportional to displacement, d2x/dt2 = -(k/m)x.
Describe SHM where a = -omega squared x, omega = 2 pi f, with solutions x = A sin(omega t) or A cos(omega t).
Use the terms simple harmonic motion, period, frequency, free and forced oscillations, resonance and damping.
Use F = kx and E = 1/2 kx squared.
Solve d2x/dt2 = -(k/m)x by numerical or graphical methods.
Use x = A sin 2 pi f t or A cos 2 pi f t.
Explain kinetic and potential energy changes in SHM as conservation of energy.
Sketch and interpret x-t, v-t and a-t graphs of SHM, including relative phases.
Use E total = 1/2 mv squared + 1/2 kx squared.
Describe free and forced vibrations, damping and resonance qualitatively.
Sketch amplitude of a resonator against driving frequency.
Practical: observe forced and damped oscillations in several systems.
Calculate the period of a mass on a spring, T = 2 pi sqrt(m/k).
Calculate the period of a simple pendulum, T = 2 pi sqrt(L/g).
Practical: measure period of a spring or pendulum and relate it to mass and length.
Explain changes of gravitational and kinetic energy.
Explain motion in a uniform gravitational field.
Explain the gravitational field and potential of a point mass, treating spheres as point masses.
Use terms gravitational field, potential and equipotential surface.
Calculate energy change mgh in a uniform field.
Calculate energy exchange and work done, noting no work along equipotentials.
Explain angular velocity in rad per second.
Explain motion in a horizontal circle and in a circular gravitational orbit.
Use a = v squared / r and F = mv squared / r = m r omega squared.
Interpret potential as area under a field-distance graph and energy change as area under a force-distance graph.
Interpret force from the tangent of a potential energy-distance graph and field strength from the tangent of a potential-distance graph.
Sketch gravitational fields and the matching equipotential surfaces.
Use F = -GMm/r squared and g = -GM/r squared.
Use gravitational potential energy -GMm/r.
Use gravitational potential -GM/r.
Explain radar-type measurement of solar-system distances, with the speed of light invariant.
Explain relativistic time dilation using gamma = 1 / sqrt(1 - v squared / c squared).
Explain measuring relative velocities by radar.
Calculate distances and relative velocities from radar-type measurements.
Describe evidence for a hot big bang from cosmological red-shift (Hubble's law) and the microwave background.
Use logarithmic scales for distance, size, mass, energy, power and brightness.
Estimate distances and ages of astronomical objects.
Explain energy transfer causing temperature change and specific thermal capacity.
Calculate temperature change using delta E = m c delta theta.
Practical: find specific thermal capacity electrically.
Explain the behaviour of ideal gases.
Explain impulse as force times time equals change in momentum.
Explain the kinetic theory of ideal gases and its assumptions.
Explain temperature as proportional to average particle energy, 3/2 kT.
Use terms ideal gas, rms speed, absolute temperature, internal energy, Avogadro, Boltzmann and gas constants, and mole.
Sketch and interpret relationships between p, V, N and T for an ideal gas.
Interpret the area under a force-time graph as impulse.
Explain the random walk of gas molecules, with displacement related to the number of steps.
Use pV = NkT with N = n N_A and Nk = nR.
Use pV = 1/3 N m c squared.
Practical: investigate the gas laws, including finding absolute zero.
Practical: investigate pressure against volume with a gauge or logger.
Explain ratios of particle numbers in states of different energy at different temperatures.
Explain how temperature affects processes with an activation energy.
Sketch and interpret graphs of the Boltzmann factor against energy and temperature.
Calculate ratios of characteristic energies to kT.
Calculate the Boltzmann factor e^(-E/kT).
Explain how a transformer works through changing flux and induced e.m.f. as rate of change of flux linkage.
Explain how a dynamo produces induced e.m.f. by relative motion of flux and conductor.
Use terms B-field, flux, flux linkage, induced e.m.f. and eddy currents.
Sketch and interpret graphs of current, flux and induced e.m.f.
Calculate flux and use Faraday's and Lenz's laws, e.m.f. = -d(N flux)/dt.
Explain electromagnetic forces qualitatively, and the force on a straight current-carrying wire in a uniform field.
Calculate F = ILB for current perpendicular to a uniform field.
Practical: find the magnetic flux density between magnet poles using a current carrier and balance.
Explain linked electric and magnetic circuits, including the roles of conductance, permeance, iron and air gaps.
Sketch lines of flux in magnetic circuits.
Use V1/V2 = N1/N2 for an ideal transformer.
Use I2/I1 = N1/N2 for an ideal transformer.
Practical: observe induced e.m.f. under varying conditions, and investigate transformers.
Explain the uniform electric field E = V/d.
Explain the field of a charged object, force on a charge, and the inverse square law.
Use terms charge, electric field, potential, equipotential surface and electronvolt.
Sketch electric fields and matching equipotential surfaces.
Calculate force and field of a point charge, F = kQq/r squared with k = 1/(4 pi epsilon0).
Explain electric potential energy and potential of a point charge, varying as 1/r.
Compare electric and gravitational fields.
Interpret potential as area under a field-distance graph and energy change as area under a force-distance graph.
Interpret force and field strength from tangents of potential energy and potential graphs.
Use E = -dV/dr, and E = V/d for uniform fields.
Calculate electrical potential energy kQq/r and potential kQ/r.
Describe evidence for discreteness of charge, such as the Millikan experiment.
Explain the force on a moving charge in a uniform magnetic field.
Calculate the force on a moving charge, F = qvB.
Explain how particle accelerators produce high-energy beams for scattering.
Explain scattering evidence for a small massive nucleus.
Sketch paths of scattered particles.
Calculate motion of a charged particle in a magnetic field with F = qvB.
Calculate kinetic and potential energy of a scattered charged particle.
Describe evidence for discrete energy levels from electron collisions or line spectra.
Describe a simple atom model as quantum electrons confined in space.
Sketch electron standing waves in simple atom models.
Describe a simple quark picture of protons and neutrons.
Balance nuclear equations using conservation of mass/energy, charge and lepton number.
Use terms energy level, scattering, nucleus, nucleon, positron, quark, gluon, neutrino, hadron, lepton, antiparticle and lepton number.
Do relativistic calculations for particles at very high speed.
Use E rest = mc squared and the relativistic factor.
Use E total = gamma E rest.
Describe ionising radiations, differences in ionising and penetrating power, and effects on living tissue.
Calculate activity of a sample from half-life or decay constant.
Calculate absorbed dose in gray as energy per unit mass.
Calculate effective dose in sievert as absorbed dose times quality factor.
Practical: study absorption of alpha, beta and gamma radiation by materials.
Practical: determine half-life of an isotope such as protactinium.
Explain nuclear stability and decay using binding energy, and the 'Nuclear Valley'.
Explain fission, chain reactions, fusion and nuclear power generation.
Use terms nucleon number, proton number, isotope, binding energy, atomic mass unit, dose and risk.
Sketch and interpret binding energy per nucleon against nucleon number.
Calculate energy changes in nuclear transformations using E = mc squared.
